nodes.question: What term is used to describe the negative emotions experienced by individuals in environmental observation roles?
nodes.paragraph: People in such roles are vulnerable to experiencing negative emotions, which could, in turn, affect their decision to keep engaging in their work and (or) other pro-environmental behaviours. We used the term eco-grief to discuss such emotions and applied a phenomenological approach to understand how environmental observers learning adjacent to ecological loss impacted their emotions, decisions, and actions. We worked with Mezirow S transformative learning as a theoretical framework, which characterizes learning through critical self-reflection and re-evaluations in perspective and connects it to decision-making and action (i.e., transformation). We categorized such learning within Mezirow S instrumental and communicative domains and attached them to the different forms of action reported by the observers. Finally, we considered how engaging in action potentially transforms emotions. Instrumental and communicative domains proved to relate to different emotional responses and forms of action, providing insight for developing programs and support for observers. Keywords Eco-anxiety Eco-grief Environmental Observers Transformative LearningAccepted: 9 February 2025 The Author(s) 2025Exploring Eco-Grief, Transformative Learning, and Action in Environmental Observers Melanie Zurba1 Polina Baum-Talmor2 Andrew Park3 Kateryna Rudenko1 Erica Mendritzki4 Roberta L Woodgate5 Lisa Binkley6 David Busolo7 1 3 Human Ecologyinvolved in environmental professions, citizen science, and other environment-observation activities, interactions with nature, and Indigenous knowledge-keeping/guardianship.

Keywords Pre-service teachers School gardens Learning gardens Connectedness to nature Environmental concernAccepted: 24 February 2025 The Author(s) 2025Connectedness to nature: assessing the impact of garden- based learning on teacher education Diego Corrochano Fern ndez1 Alejandro G mez-Gon alves1 Sara Serrate Gonz lez1 Jos Manuel Mu OZ Rodr guez1 Diego Corrochano Fern ndez dcf@usal.es Alejandro G mez-Gon alves algomez@usal.es Sara Serrate Gonz lez sarasg@usal.es Jos Manuel Mu OZ Rodr guez pepema@usal.es 1 Universidad de Salamanca, Salamanca, Spain 13 Journal of Outdoor and Environmental EducationIntroduction The planet is facing a global environmental crisis that is mainly linked to the effects of climate change, pollution, and biodiversity loss. To ensure a sustainable future requires a joint and systematic approach to these problems. In this regard, educa - tion is essential to the political and economic transformation that is needed (Baste et al., 2021 ). Despite the efforts engaged in over the last decades, education for sus - tainability and environmental education as genuine training for sustainable devel - opment still require improvement, since the future of our environment depends on the decisions made by future generations (Murga-Menoyo, 2021 ).

nodes.question: What challenges have environmental issues raised regarding society and politics?
nodes.answer: They have raised questions concerning the ability of society and politics to cope with environmental challenges, particularly in liberal democracies.
nodes.paragraph: Whilethe impact of these forms of con ict management, bridge- building, or even cooperation may vary, they altogether de ne the nature of local interactive governance and itscapacities for promoting sustainable development and democracy. Keywords Interactive governance /C1Local climate governance /C1Civil society /C1 Local administration /C1 Collaboration Introduction While environmental challenges are high on the publicagenda, they have raised many questions concerning the ability of society and politics to cope with them. Much ofthe attention goes either to government action or to the various forms of people S reaction, namely protest on the streets and at the voting ballots. Especially liberaldemocracies, claiming to bridge people S will and institu- tional politics, get distressed by the massive challenges of the environmental crisis. The respective routines andinstitutions of democratic governance, as well as their methods of intermediating between institutional politics and the people, are being subjected to scrutiny. There is asearch for more interactive forms and proceedings that can mitigate con ict and dissent and facilitate the creation of legitimate and ef cient environmental politics. This calls for a relational approach (Evers & von Essen, 2019 & 2024 ), that takes up the roles of civic engagement and civil society actors as part of a wider complex interplay between state (political and administrative institutions), civil soci- ety, and economy.
